speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: POSSIBLE REDUCTION IN SALES TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It arises out of some questions I asked the other day relative to a suggestion in the press that the U.S.S.R. would not be buying much more Canadian wheat. I would ask the right hon. gentleman whether his attention has been directed to a statement made yesterday by Mr. Khrushchev in Odense, Denmark, as follows:
It is unlikely Moscow will make further purchases of grain from the west which has provided millions of bushels of wheat to offset poor Russian crops of 1963.
This is a matter that is very important to the economy of Canada. Is the Prime Minister in a position to say what discussions have taken place in this connection, and whether there is sound reason to fear that the U.S.S.R. will be greatly reducing, if not entirely ending, the contracts for the purchase of wheat?

maintopic: POSSIBLE REDUCTION IN SALES TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is of course a very important question; it is a question of long range significance. I will have to wait until the return of the Minister of Trade and Commerce today, and perhaps he will be in a position to make a statement on the whole matter early next week.

maintopic: POSSIBLE REDUCTION IN SALES TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wanted to ask the Prime Minister, in view of the uncertainty of continuing wheat sales to the U.S.S.R., if the government would expedite its policy of foreign aid in order to take up some of the slack in wheat exports later this year.

maintopic: POSSIBLE REDUCTION IN SALES TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
I will be very glad to look into that situation, Mr. Speaker. I was not quite sure that I heard the hon. member's question correctly, but I think it was that we should
expedite and increase foreign aid. Certain steps have already been taken in this connection, and if the situation requires it and makes it possible, more steps could be taken.

maintopic: POSSIBLE REDUCTION IN SALES TO RUSSIA
speechtext: The government have announced that they intend to step up foreign aid, particularly in food exports, to some-think like $40 million a year. I am asking the government now if they will take some action to implement this stated policy of theirs to take up some of the slack.

maintopic: POSSIBLE REDUCTION IN SALES TO RUSSIA

Most Gracious Sovereign:

An act to amend the British North America Act 1867.
Whereas the Senate and House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled have submitted an address to Her Majesty praying that Her Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom for the enactment of the provisions hereinafter set forth:
Be it therefore enacted by the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:
Amendment as to legislation respecting old age pensions. 30 & 31 Viet., c. 3; 9 Eliz. II, c. 2.
1. Section ninety four A of the British North America Act, 1867 is hereby repealed and the following substituted therefor:

Legislation respecting old age pensions and supplementary benefits.
"94A. The parliament of Canada may make laws in relation to old age pensions and supplementary benefits, including survivors' and disability benefits irrespective of age, but no such law shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to any such matter."
Short title and citation.

speechtext:
Shortly before government business was suspended last evening for royal assent proceedings, when the house was considering a motion by the right hon. Prime Minister for the presentation of an address requesting a constitutional amendment, the hon. member for Villeneuve moved in amendment thereto the following:
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rober-val (Mr. Gauthier), that the following words be added to section 94A after the words "to any such matter": "but this amendment to the British North America Act does apply only to those provinces who will ask for it".
A number of hon. members were considerate, enough to offer their views on the legality of the amendment. As I pointed out last night, many of the arguments put forward either in support of or in opposition to the amendment touched on the constitutional aspect of the matter rather than on the very limited procedural aspect that must be of concern to the Chair in accepting or rejecting the motion.
The hon. member for Lapointe made a very interesting contribution to the discussion. He argued that this amendment proposed by the hon. member for Villeneuve is constitutional. He said in particular, as reported at page 4671 of the French edition of Hansard:

I say that the subamendment is constitutional and that it completes the other one because it bears no relation to the legislation which the government proposes to introduce this year concerning old age pensions.
It is a complementary amendment because it is connected with the future legislation that the federal government will wish to move as regards the Old Age Pensions Act; it will also permit the government to legislate on the supplementary benefits, including survivors and disability benefits, irrespective of age.
And further on:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that to save a principle is far more important that all the arguments put forward by representatives of the four other parties. We must save the principle that, in such fields, in provincial fields, the federal government should never be able to take action without
British North America Act the consent or the agreement of the provinces, more particularly of the province of Quebec.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I believe you should declare the amendment in order.
The suggestion that the amendment is constitutionally acceptable or that it deserves the support of the house as to its principle, does not, I think, mean that it is necessarily acceptable as far as standing orders are concerned.
An amendment is out of order from the procedural standpoint if it contradicts the main motion it is intended to amend. In the remarks he made last night, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) said:
-I submit that the amendment is entirely out of order, because it is contrary to the very nature of the subject matter and also because it would render meaningless the aim and object of the resolution now under consideration.
The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul), the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapdelaine) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) were of the same opinion.

May I refer particularly to the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who said in part, as reported at page 4479 of Hansard, when speaking to this amendment:
It is not relevant in that it says that it does not apply to the provinces. Section 94A does not apply to the provinces either. This is an amendment giving the federal parliament power; and when an hon. member comes along with an amendment which says that it does not apply to the provinces unless that is asked for, our problem is that it does not seem to make any sense in English or in French.
I should like to refer hon. members to citation 203(1) of the fourth edition of Beau-chesne, page 171, which reads as follows:
Every amendment proposed to be made either to a question or to a proposed amendment should be so framed that if agreed to by the house the question or amendment as amended would be intelligible and consistent with itself.
I also refer hon. members to citation 202, paragraph 12, which reads as follows:
An amendment proposing a direct negative, though it may be covered up by verbiage-
I might say I am not too enthusiastic about the word "verbiage". It seems to have a rather strong connotation which I would not like to apply to the amendment proposed by the hon. member.

An amendment was moved that the house welcomed certain terms of the agreement and condemned several features of it. The Speaker ruled it out because (a) the portion of the amendment which approved the agreement was useless as it suggested no change in the main motion, and also, (b) an amendment to disapprove what the main motion approves is nothing but an expanded negative.

However, the mere fact that this proposal is now before the house puts very severe doubt on the sincerity of certain members of the government and certain other members in stating that there were survivorship benefits in the former plan. I am trying to set out the approach I take to this amendment and the reasons we should, or should not, apply for it.
I should like to consider the bits and pieces of this plan which are now before us. The first is Bill No. C-75, which is on the order
British North America Act paper. I am sure this will have to be withdrawn and a new one presented, because the form of the plan has been radically changed. The second is the resolution on the order paper to set up a committee. It is not properly worded to suit the new plan, and I assume it will have to be withdrawn, or amended, or that some other action will have to be taken. In any case it does give the government the chance to proceed with a reference to a committee.
I wonder whether the intentions of the government are still the same as they were before it was decided to seek these amendments. At first, perhaps, the government was anxious for the committee to bail it out of its difficulties; the Prime Minister consented to the committee having the broadest terms of reference so as to be able to make reports on questions of principle. I believe he had in mind a vague hope that the committee would throw the bill back and say "No, we must have these disability and survivors' benefits". Now that the course has changed, I wonder whether the government still wishes the committee to have such broad terms of reference. We do not know, because we are in a completely new situation.
The third difficulty arises from the innumerable exchanges of letters between the Prime Minister and the premiers of the provinces. I have examined the parliamentary records and find there are a great number of returns in connection with the Canada pension plan. There are many letters. There is sessional paper No. 202-J, filed on June 10, which is the most recent. There are others which contain copies of letters written by the Prime Minister to private individuals and to provincial premiers. There have been two white papers filed, in addition to the bill, and we wonder which of these documents and letters are applicable to the proposed new plan, which of these undertakings we can now consider to be live. In addition, I wonder what other letters, documents or statements are still outstanding, papers which no one has been wise enough to ask for, or which have not yet been made public.
I think the Canada pension plan is in a state of disarray as far as the papers are concerned. I believe the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare must have nightmares about the undertakings which may come back to haunt them when the plan is finally brought before the house.
Not only is the plan itself, the physical condition of the plan, in disarray; so is its

British North America Act application. The first thing I would like to point out is that the provinces now have four alternatives if the present proposal is put into effect. First, they can permit the Canada pension plan to be operated by the federal government within the province. Second, the province itself can operate the Canada pension plan within the province and administer the funds and the plan. Third, the province can operate its own plan on a basis that would make it portable with the Canada pension plan; that is, making its minimum provisions approximately the same so that a person may go from province to province and have some portability of pension. Finally, a province can ignore the Canada pension plan and operate completely outside it.
This latter point is confirmed, mainly in principle, by the vote we had this morning on the amendment. I do not wish to say anything more about that, but the fact is that even the amendment for which we are asking does not exclude a province either now or in the future from bringing in its own plan having no relationship whatsoever to the Canada pension plan.
This is the ludicrous position the Canada pension plan is now in. There are four alternatives for the provinces to adopt. Which one, or which combinations of plans, will each of the provinces adopt? I would hope -and I am not saying these things for the purpose of causing trouble-that when this is all sorted out the provinces can be persuaded to implement something which will constitute a national plan. But certainly, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing of that type in evidence now.
Just to illustrate my point let me say this. Having got Quebec into this whole deal, Quebec is now out. The plan that Quebec proposed has been, in substance, accepted by the federal government, although I know that in the provincial legislature there is some difference of opinion between Mr. Lesage and Mr. Johnson. Mr. Lesage says that Ottawa followed his plan and Mr. Johnson says that Mr. Lesage followed Ottawa's plan. Kegard-less of which of these allegations may be true, there is still some time in which to consider these two plans. We have to ascertain whether the Quebec plan will be portable with the plans which other provinces now have in readiness. I think particularly of Ontario, and of the province of Saskatchewan. Will these plans be portable?

Then what about private plans, Mr. Speaker? This is the most recent difficulty that has arisen. We have heard that the province of Quebec intends to take over the registration and control of private plans that will operate outside the Canada pension plan. I am not sure how far this will go, but it does point up the difficulty that we are going to encounter in the need to tie in private plans with the Canada pension plan. Where are these plans going to be tied in? We have no direction on this whatsoever. In addition to the four alternatives the provinces have with regard to public plans, they have just as many alternatives with regard to private plans. Ontario has in readiness a plan for portability; it should come into effect at the beginning of next year.

subtopic: ADDRESS REQUESTING AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR SURVIVORS' AND DISABILITY BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before one o'clock I was interrupted by the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro), who took exception to my previous statement that he had tried to give the impression that there were survivorship benefits in the former pension plan. His intervention on a question of privilege I took to be an effort to prove that he did know all the time that the previous pension plan was no good. In the result he proved the very point I was trying to make, which was that with full knowledge that the former plan was not satisfactory he nevertheless continued to give the public the general impression that the plan was wonderful.
I was discussing, Mr. Speaker, the question of private pension plans when I was interrupted. The government has dipped into matters of provincial jurisdiction to bring on the benefits of a pension plan, but they do not want the responsibility of the private pension plan problems. They just invade the provincial field far enough to create a problem in connection with private pension plans, but not to the point of giving any assistance to help solve the problem they have created. They say to the provinces: "We are bringing forward a national plan which we want you to accept, because it is beneficial". To this point the present legislation and proposals go; but having reached that point and created problems for private plans all across the country, the government stop there and say to the provinces: "Well, this question of private plans really is not our responsibility; it is yours, so you solve it the best way you can".
Just before one o'clock I stated my contention that this is not a satisfactory way of solving the problem. There are four alternatives the provinces can take in connection with the national plan. There are just as many or even more alternatives that can be taken in connection with private plans. My point is that the situation is going to be so


confused that there will not be any national plan or any uniformity in pensions across Canada.
I am seriously concerned, Mr. Speaker, about the economic effects of this whole plan. So far as a pension plan provides a vehicle for compulsory savings for retirement, I can see no objection in principle. I think it is a worthy effort to encourage, in fact to compel in some cases, people to save for their retirement years and for their future. To this extent I have no objection, and to the point to which this plan goes it is a worthy effort. But the trouble now is that this plan has gone far beyond what one would call a compulsory savings plan; it is developing into something else.
I should like to express the situation by saying that the plan now is not a pension plan but a pension deal. In other words, it is based on the result of bargains which have been struck all over the place and is not the result of a calm and considered pension plan. This is not the time to go into details, Mr. Speaker, but there are departures from the basic set-up for pensions which have gone far beyond what I believe to be suitable for a national pension plan. These changes are alarming. The escalation of benefits is much too steep for any actuarial plan, or for anything approaching an actuarial plan, to be suitable; and the new plan is making them much steeper. The widows' benefits are calculated on a double standard. They start off on a price index basis for a certain period of time, the first ten years, then they go on to a wage index and finally, when the widow becomes of pensionable age under the Old Age Security Act, they go back to a price index basis. This is a most confusing method of calculating a widow's allowance. She has no knowledge from one day to the next what the amount of her pension will be or the method by which it will be calculated in the future.
There are many other things which I do not wish to go into now. My point is that the plan is now in such a very difficult state, both from an actuarial and physical point of view, it is difficult to know whether any actuarial basis will result in the end or whether, in reality, this will become another welfare scheme. This is what many people feared in the beginning, that it might become another welfare scheme and not a compulsory savings plan. We appear now to be coming to the point where it will be a combination of both and nothing much of either.

I say, Mr. Speaker, there are too many tag ends lying around. The whole situation is very confused. We should really have another white paper so that we will know where we are, and we should have had one before this debate commenced. We had a white paper in July, 1963, setting out the Canada pension plan. We had another white paper in March, 1964, setting out another pension plan. One of my colleagues suggests that the white paper is now getting a little grey. As I pointed out in the beginning, it is difficult to know exactly where we are with this particular pension plan at this moment.
In concluding, may I say that the time is opportune for a constitutional amendment. I think we must pass it now and deal with the problem of the Canada pension plan as a secondary matter. To that extent, therefore, I support the motion before us.

Mr. Speaker, hon. members who have participated in this debate before me have made reference to the anomalous situation which existed when we interrupted the debate with regard to national symbols which have been proposed for this country and found ourselves faced with the very extraordinary position of having, within the terms of the motion we are now discussing, to humbly approach Her Majesty praying that she may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before parliament, and so on. Now, all hon. members who have discussed this have said how ironical it is, and I do not think it is necessary to enlarge on that except to make this point wihch I think is a necessary corollary to be drawn from what has been said.
Hon. members have said, let us hope that this situation will not again occur; let us hope that before too long we will have domiciled in Canada the constitution for which we now seek changes in the United Kingdom. I say, Mr. Speaker, that I see little prospect of that. I believe I am entitled to mention this point at this time. I see little prospect of that because of the fact that during the course of the last year there have been deep and strong currents of hostility sweeping across this land, and the very debate which we interrupted, in my opinion- I will say more about this on a more appropriate occasion, but I think I must say it here- has hardened or deepened these emotions

British North America Act across our country to the point where violent emotions may yet sweep over this land and prevent the degree of unity which we must have if we are going to have the constitution returned to Canada.
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), in his unusual approach to this problem, indicated that a measure of unanimity would be required before we could even at the very least bring the constitution back to Canada. I say, is there any hon. member in this house who honestly believes that the situation which now exists will not be so reflected in any constitutional conference with the provinces that the prospect of obtaining unanimity has been put back for years, if not for generations? Whether we like it or not, because of this fact, it is my opinion from what I have observed and read that when we come to consider further amendments, because of what happened last year and particularly in the last few weeks we will still be going through this process of humbly asking Her Majesty to have her parliament in Westminster amend our constitution, when the need next arises. I was very glad to hear the Prime Minister say this morning, in response to a question, that this matter will be placed on the agenda for the next federal-provincial conference. However, I would point out that some time ago I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), who would be the member of the government most concerned, whether or not in his opinion the time was ripe to reconvene the constitutional conference of the attorneys general, about which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke, when he said that in 1960 and 1961 such great progress had been made. I think the Minister of Justice is a realisitic man and so in his answer he said not only had no date been fixed but that no formal letter had been sent out suggesting that a date be fixed. It might well be that the minister has been alerted as a result of my question, and I hope he is now sending out a letter for that purpose.
However, I do make the statement in all seriousness that the situation which has existed, which does exist and will continue to exist, in my humble opinion will make it most difficult, if not impossible for some considerable time, for us to secure the things we need; and all the brave and bold words, all the ringing terms and stirring declarations in the very fine debate on the flag question are, to my way of thinking, so much waste because of this situation.

I generally accept the principle in this motion, but I must say I hinge a qualification, an attaching condition, that I do not think it should be assumed that because we are accepting and approving the motion for this address to be forwarded to Her Majesty, we also accept with it, as the tail of the comet, the principles of the proposed pension legislation about which we have heard from time to time from members of the government.
Reference has been made to this by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken). I am not going to say any more about it, except to suggest a very good expression is one which we used in the front lines during the last war, when the brass in the field and the brass on the staff had got together and had thoroughly messed up the situation. We used to say it was "snafu"-situation normal, all fouled up. I think this is about as good a description as the pension legislation situation is worth at this time.
But I say in approaching this motion-and there are some other qualifications-I do so on the distinct understanding that it does not indicate by any means a wholehearted approval of the pension legislation. It is my opinion that a large percentage of the people of Canada have come to the decision that some type of contributory pension plan is desirable. On the other hand, when the legislation is laid before us it will be our duty to examine it as to its reasonableness, as to the degree of contribution required, and as to whether or not it will lay a burden upon the economy of the country that the country can well bear, having in mind all its other responsibilities. These are matters upon which we must reserve our decision until the appropriate time, and in approving the motion this, with other qualifications, must be the first condition attached.
Now, let us look at the proposed amendment itself. I have some doubts as to whether, having in mind it was essential for the government to secure this constitutional amendment, it might not well have gone further and done better, and possibly saved the necessity of coming back here again. In the first place this amendment purports to repeal and replace section 94A of the British North America Act.
I call to the attention of hon. members that the position of section 94A must be of some significance. Sections 91, 92 and 93 deal with exclusive rights, given respectively to the federal and provincial governments as the case may be. However, sections

94A and 95 deal with what is in effect concurrent legislation, where both federal and provincial governments have been given rights to legislate. In section 95, as hon. members know, the provinces are given the right to legislate in respect of agriculture and immigration, and so is the federal government; but it is laid down that where there is a conflict-as necessarily there would be a conflict if you have legislation on these subjects by distinctive legislatures-the federal government legislation must prevail. This is placed immediately after section 94A, which also gives rights to both provincial and federal governments to legislate; but there the reverse is the case, and provincial legislation must be dominant.
The section as it now reads, and this particular part has been carried on in the new, proposed amendment:
-no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
In order to establish a foundation for the point I propose to make I would like to refer hon. members to the amendment in its present form, which was brought forth in 1951. At that time there was an exchange of correspondence between the then minister of justice, Mr. Garson, and the provincial premiers, and the original proposition made by Mr. Garson was contained in the form of a proposed amendment quite distinct from section 94A as it now appears. It was as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, the parliament of Canada may make laws in relation to old age pensions.
And there it stopped. In other words, the original amendment as suggested was an amendment which, in the view of many of the attorneys general of the provinces and of the premiers of the provinces, expressed in the correspondence tabled in this house in 1951, gave to the federal government not necessarily exclusive but certainly paramount jurisdiction in the field of pension laws. I think it was probably wise that this should have been the case, and this is the first point I make, that I would have much preferred this amendment to have eliminated the words which appear there, that-
-no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
It is my submission that by leaving this portion in as it now appears, we are putting in the hands of the provinces the right of
British North America Act any province at any time to veto by means of enacting legislation, which is distinct in any material respect from the federal legislation, and so prevent the federal legislation from operating in that province.
Let me give an illustration of that. I have before me a news item from the Montreal Gazette of June 17, 1964, dealing with when this matter was being debated in the legislature of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Johnson, the leader of the official opposition in the legislature in Quebec, is reported in this way: "Johnson Says Pension Plan Socially Bad". He is reported as giving a number of reasons which he thinks are sound why this is not good legislation and why in its present form it should not be carried out. I simply put the case in this way. If Mr. Johnson thinks that the legislation which the province of Quebec now desires, which is comparable to and parallel with the legislation and the plan of the federal government, is bad legislation, then if he should secure power in a future election in the province of Quebec he will repeal or amend it. The minute he does that it will be legislation distinct in form from the legislation that the federal government has passed and consequently the federal plan will no longer be operative.
I think this can apply in any province. Any leader of a political party seeking power in a province might, if I may use a distinguished parallel, make a promise on the election platform that within two years after being elected he will bring before the legislature a distinctive provincial plan and then upon securing power bring into effect this distinctive provincial plan whereupon the federal plan must immediately fall to the ground.
Section 94A relating to old age pensions probably did not present any particular difficulty as it stood, because under our pension legislation up to this time it has been a matter of the federal government making a payment at the age set by statute, which payment has been increased from time to time; and actually there have been no rights accruing, save possibly general legislative rights with respect to individuals in the country who reach this age. But on the basis of a contributory pension plan it is my submission that an entirely different situation will prevail. There will be contributions made form workers' salaries and by employers. Large funds will be accumulated which will be susceptible of being used for development purposes. The people living in each province will acquire distinct, specific vested rights in

British North America Act contributory pension plans. Then instead of that degree of permanency which must be present to ensure the success of a contributory pension plan, the position will be that at any time a provincial government sees fit to introduce legislation of this nature which is at variance with the federal plan the provincial legislation will then prevail.
While I support this address, I should like to have seen it provided that in the event of there being any conflict between federal and provincial legislation the federal plan must prevail, and I think in due course the government will find it will have to come to this, if it can ever secure that degree of unanimity to which I referred before. Whether we like it or not, if we are going to have a sound, successful, permanent plan I suggest that we will have to bring ourselves to this position.
There is one other point I should like to make before I resume my seat. The new section 94A is to read in part as follows:
The parliament of Canada may make laws in relation to old age pensions and supplementary benefits, including survivors' and disability benefits-
I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) and others say that the law officers of the crown have indicated in the past that the use of the term "old age pensions" is sufficiently wide to include a scheme of contributory pensions. I accept that the law officers of the crown are distinguished and knowledgeable members of my profession, and I certainly do not propose to set my views up in complete opposition to theirs. But as a member of the house I must say that some doubt runs in my mind with regard to whether or not it would not have been better to have eliminated the words "old age" and substituted the word "contributory" or else use the words "old age and contributory pensions".
I look at the matter in this way. What is old age? When does old age start? At what stage of a man's or woman's life does old age begin? I see the Prime Minister smiling at that. It may be that the process of aging goes on a little more rapidly in this house than in other places. But let us assume that at some time in the future it may be desirable to reduce the age at which the contributory pensions are paid. We do not know when that will be desirable or when it will be financially feasible. We may find that from an age of 65 we will come down to 62, 60 or even less than 60. Are these pensions then old age pensions? Can they be brought under

the description now appearing in section 94A, that "the parliament of Canada may make laws in relation to old age pensions"?
I submit with respect that there is very grave doubt in that regard. While we were in the process of securing a constitutional amendment I think we should have gone the whole distance and used such words as "old age and contributory pensions". It may be suggested that follows from the use of the words "old age pensions and supplementary benefits" but I think that the word "supplementary" must be related to "old age" and that the legal principle of ejusdem generis applies. I doubt that you can use this particular phrase to say that a pension payable at a lower age than what might be considered old age is a pension included in this legislation.
There is no doubt at all that some of the best legal minds in the country are going to be scrutinizing this constitutional amendment and examining the legislation which the government proposes to introduce. I say that if we are going to have pension legislation we should leave nothing to chance. In my thinking there are defects in this proposal. While I support the address I feel it is my duty to say that I think there are defects, and these defects will appear in the future.

Let me be a little more specific. If I may go back to the legislation for a pension plan brought in by the Conservative party, the Liberals put forward strong criticism that an amendment such as is now being put forward by that party was not necessary. If you will examine the speeches you will find that one after the other they got up and said it was not necessary. They pooh-poohed the idea all along the line, but now they are

faced with the fact that they have to ask for such an amendment. That is the first point.
Let us take the history of their production of a plan. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) brought in a plan last year. She brought in another plan and it was more or less dropped and, indeed, most of us-and this expresses the reservations put forward today-are wondering just how far this government has gone in getting its legislation properly prepared and looking into the future. Premier Lesage could not make a speech quickly enough and could not get to the press quickly enough, when the initial plan was put forward, to say: Count me out; I am not with this; there has been no consultation whatsoever. In the field of diplomacy, I do not know what the Prime Minister was thinking about but it is perfectly obvious
British North America Act that after a short time his people told him he had better get the concurrence of those provinces, otherwise the plan as a national plan would be a flop.
We read lately in the newspapers, and it was trumpeted by various members of the Liberal party, what a tremendous diplomatic job had been done. speechtext:
I have a few remarks to make on this question. They will not be along the lines followed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) or by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). They deal with another aspect of this subject.
The question before us raises the whole question of national sovereignty. It portrays vividly the source and origin of our constitu-


tion. The British North America Act distinguishes Canada as a unit, a nation, a people. The B.N.A. Act outlines the guarantees and protections provided to the elements which compose that union. Upon these articles contained in the Act of Union of 1867, the one-nation concept was adopted. The necessity of proceeding to Westminster to amend our constitution is a relic of the suspicions and fears of the generation before confederation. It is the only remaining symbol to mark our immaturity as a nation. It, more than any other thing, has delayed and prevented the welding of interest which might otherwise have brought Canadians together.
It is a remarkable achievement that confederation has been able to survive under the handicap contained in this particle of immaturity. Confederation has survived. Confederation has spread from four to ten provinces and two territories. Each of the four, and each of the others, can measure the sacrifice voluntarily assumed and suffered to achieve our present status. This measure before us today reminds us all that a great mutual trust and respect is required if we are to be liberated from this relic of the past.
That is for Canadians to choose for themselves. The new Canadians, from which my family originates, have been ready and even eager for Canada to take unto herself the right to determine her own constitution. We believe it would be a step along the way to national unity and national purpose; it would complete the foundations upon which this nation could choose and develop those symbols that could rally our people in the building of this nation.
The Canada of 1964 is not the Canada of 1867. Throughout the years one thing has remained unchanged. Confederation has held a common objective for all Canadians. In the beginning divergent elements joined in a common purpose. Their decision was a deliberate one, despite their differences. They must have known that conflict might arise in an emerging nation. That much this generation owes in tribute to the spirit and tolerance of those days, as revealed by the articles of confederation. That union has admitted new loyalties, and I have the abiding courage to believe that union continues as the greatest inspiration on which people in every part of Canada have to draw on.
The concept of the one nation is, if anything, more urgent and desirable today than ever before. The nations of the world no longer can feel secure in their own separate

worlds. Why then should the cry of separatism within a nation hope to achieve anything but a lesser security and recognition by following the paths of division? The cry of the separatist is the cry of those who say, "You have nothing to lose". It is a negative cry; it is a denial of courage and purpose of the generation that chose confederation. It measures the extent to which the fires of isolation have been fed and nurtured. Confederation still beckons; the opportunities it offers return again and again, providing the opportunity for wholesome participation in the building of a greater Canada. The years have passed, since 1867, like dropping leaves, and have left a tree somewhat more naked than any of us would like to see. The history of those years cannot be rewritten; it will always be with us as a nation. Surely we can make a new beginning. That is one of the reasons I am proud to be a member of this party now constituting the official opposition in parliament. This party has not been ready to barter the heritage of Canadians. Our leader has never sought to isolate the people in any area of Canada. His hands have never reached to feed the fires of division and isolation. His invitation has always been participation, not separation. Equality within confederation requires participation. Participation yields the fruits of recognition. That is the path upon which Canadians can leave the imprint of their identity and personality. That is the emerging nation, sought and promised by confederation.
That being so, sir, I wish to take this opportunity to renew the request for a joint conference of provincial and federal government officials to study our constitution for the purpose of providing a new beginning for confederation and the elements that now comprise confederation as we know it. This party and my leader, the Leader of the Opposition, were ready to proceed along these lines when we were swept from office. I urge the present Prime Minister to unfetter himself from the tortuous course he has been embarked upon and give recognition to the positive fruits of confederation by calling together a full-fledged conference to deal with the matters of confederation. Of course, Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of this resolution as it is and I join with those others of my party in the remarks they have made regarding it.

British North America Act As a consequence, Mr. Speaker, we are heartily in accord with the passing of this resolution to enact an amendment to the British North America Act. I remember the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) when I held the portfolio of national health and welfare criticizing us to the extent of saying this amendment would not be necessary. I am intrigued by the present plan as it unfolds. And then according to the Montreal Gazette of June 11 the Prime Minister again added more details. Therefore, we are most anxious to see what this new over-all completed plan will entail. I imagine there will be a white paper prepared on this newest and latest plan, and of course it will have to be given a great deal of study. Well, Mr. Speaker, I did see one or two members asleep but some of them have just awakened. I do not intend to take very much time, but I do not think that I have spoken on this amendment to our constitution on any other occasion and I should like to say a few words with regard to it. I feel today-and I think it is time somebody said this-that when we take a really cold look at our constitution, as we should do so at a time like this when asking for an amendment to the constitution in connection with survivor benefits, we realize we have wandered somewhat astray from the intention of the fathers of confederation. There was no doubt at that time when they were considering union, about which I shall have something to say in few minutes, that there was the question posed as to whether we should have a legislative union or a


federal union. A legislative union, as we all know, would have put most of the powers into the central government which would have been delegated to the various provincial governments. The alternative was a division of powers in a federal system, such as that finally adopted. Then they ran into difficulty at the first conference in 1864 and at the second conference in Quebec, and a compromise was reached between Sir John A. Macdonald and Cartier on a federal union.
In a federal union certain powers are put in the central government and other powers are delegated to provincial governments. Unfortunately this federal type of system, which was, as I have said, a compromise reached between Macdonald and Cartier, has had serious repercussions. At one time when our constitution went before the Supreme Court of Canada and the judicial committee of the privy council, the interpretation given to the constitution was that it took certain powers away from the central government and strengthened the provincial government. When this system is compared with the federal system of the United States one finds that their courts interpreted the powers away from the states and made the central government stronger.
The charge I am making against the Liberal party-and here I speak for myself as a member of parliament and not as a member of any particular party-is this. It may be a passing phase of Liberalism under Pearson, which I call a wishy-washy type of Liberalism, but in order to reach certain compromises-although some people call this diplomacy-the Liberal government brought in a pension plan three times and then withdrew it. The point I am making is that if this country is to survive in confederation we have to make certain that we have a strong federal administration. We must have a strong central government at Ottawa. The kind of federalism which we have today is a balkanization of Canada which I believe was never intended. If this country is to survive we cannot have ten distinct governments dictating every time to the federal authorities. We must delegate to Ottawa some supremacy.
With regard to amending the constitution, we have just heard the last two speakers and also the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), in which he properly put forward the fact that this party realized that when dealing with survivor benefits we must have an amendment to our constitution.

We had the consent of all ten provinces except Quebec. If we are to have the kind of constitution which can only be amended with the consent of all provinces, then this puts our constitution in the middle of the political field.
Why do I say that, Mr. Speaker? Well, we happen to have in Quebec today a premier who is not sympathetic, and if it were not for the fact that he dictates his own terms to this government we would probably never be here today arguing this point. I take the position that Lesage is running the government of Canada, not the present Prime Minister or the Liberals who sit opposite.

Someone says shame. Of course it is a shame. It has always been a shame. But the fact is that the constitution is put in the middle of politics. Why? We would never have got an amendment in the development and evolution of our democratic principles unless we had a sympathetic government in certain provinces with federal authority. Therefore, in order to amend our constitution we have to have the same parties in certain provinces as we have in Ottawa. Surely this is not good enough, and it certainly was not the intention of the fathers of confederation, who had a greater dream than that.
The first thing to do, Mr. Speaker, and I know it has to be done in this way because there is some expediency for it, is that instead of spending days on arguing about a flag when there are so many other important things to do, particularly when there is a sensitivity in confederation, we should come to grips with the problem of amending our constitution on a sound legal basis. Surely if we are to have the contract system in order to amend our constitution, when there are ten parties to the contract it should not be the kind of contract where in law, if you wish to change it, you have to get the consent of all parties to the contract. If we have a democracy at all in this country this should be done by majority rule. For example, if nine or eight of the provinces want to amend the constitution, and it is important to Canadians that this be done-whether it be in the field of welfare or health or any other field- surely the majority of Canadians should be able to say to the government of the country or to whatever authority exists having jurisdiction over the constitution that it should be so amended. That is the first point I want to make and we should take a hard look at 20220-287
British North America Act this problem. We are worrying about the flag and spending a lot of time debating the issue. Surely the thing we should have been considering, if we want to be an independent and great nation with all the sovereignty we dream and speak about with such great emotion, is giving the country the right to amend its own constitution, and doing so on this side of the ocean. If you read what Mr. St. Laurent said during his term of office about the various manners in which you can amend the constitution, I am sure you will find that he felt then the same as I feel at this time. It is a far more important thing that we have the ability to amend our own constitution.
I come back to the other point, that it is unfortunate we did not obtain the ability to amend our constitution when the imperial parliament passed the act in 1867 making this nation. When I am talking about the nation, I am sorry that my friend in the corner whom I call the "little Beauehesne" is not here. I am one of those people who believe that confederation was not the union of two nations; it was the union of four colonies who united at that time and who realized their destinies individually by combining to create a nation. It may have been, and indeed it was, a union of two great cultures, the French on the one hand and the English on the other. My friends opposite laugh, but they only laugh because they have never dusted off the pages of history or read the debates that took place at that time.
If they want to try to explore the real birth certificate of our nation, then they should look at the pages of history. They will find that it was the four colonies who united. The earliest meetings relating to confederation were not held in the province of Quebec or in the province of Ontario. The first meetings were held in the maritimes. The first real problem we had with confederation did not relate to Upper or Lower Canada but to the fact that Nova Scotia wished to withdraw. I do not want to take the time this afternoon to go through history to show that the birth of our nation was the result of the union of four colonies. There was just as distinctive a culture in the maritimes as there was in Quebec. There was just as distinctive a culture in Ontario as there was in Quebec. If you look at the pages of history you will see that at the time the northwest was controlled by the Hudson's Bay Company. These men had a great vision. The culture of the northwest likewise would be a part of our way of life.

British North America Act I should like now to quote from a historian, George W. Brown. Sometimes when we get so far off the track it is best to ascertain what the real facts of history are, especially when there is this talk across the country that spreads dissension and disunity. I quote from Mr. Brown's book:
"Sir, it is my fervent aspiration and hope that some here tonight may live to see the day when the-
-flag shall proudly wave from Labrador to Vancouver island, and from Niagara to the shores of Hudson bay." So spoke the Canadian leader, George Brown, in 1858. Lord Durham and others had also dreamed of a united British American nation, but in the 1850's it was still nothing but a dream.
We only have to walk in the door of the House of Commons to find out what our history is. These words of Durham, these words of Brown, the words of Cartier and Macdonald are spelled out quite simply over the entrance as we come into this House of Commons. This is the reason I say it never was the union of two nations, it was the union of four colonies. It was the vision of these men that we would become a great nation. People came to this land from various parts of the world. They came from Europe to carve out a new destiny. Why did they come? There had been wars and fears of wars in Europe and this left in the bosom of these people hatred and animosities. When they came to Canada they set aside those animosities and those prejudices. They came to live with one another as neighbours and to build the nation, Canada.
I should like to quote again from the historian, Mr. George Brown. I ask every one of you, if you have not done so before, to take a look above the door as you enter the House of Commons. Carved in stone above the main door of the parliament buildings of Canada are these words, "The wholesome sea is at her gates, her gates both east and west." This is the situation. We are in a period of sensitivity for confederation. We are in a period of sensitivity for confederation because of the ambitions, because of the desires of a certain group who, for their own political purposes, would like to carve up this nation rather than unite. We had people of this type back in 1864 when we were trying to get together. Every time the Liberals enter the gates of office, we have a period of sensitivity for confederation. As one distinguished member said last night, they have a habit of pitting the French against the English, one


religion against another. We have a sensitivity of confederation and in that period of sensitivity we must not forget one thing when we are dealing with amendments to our constitution. It is time somebody stood up in this house and said it. This nation can only last as long as we have a strong central government. Even under federalism you must have a strong central government. The Liberals are like the waves of the ocean-they roll with the tides.
During the war and after the war, they believed in centralizing everything. Today, in order to buy the votes of certain provinces in this country of ours they now say we must have a weak government. It1 is time we adopted the same principles in respect of our constitution that were used to carve out this land in 1867, the same principles that were followed to solve the depression of the thirties and which brought us through two wars. As I said at the beginning, we should have the right to amend our constitution on this side of the ocean.
Now, I have said something about confederation and I want to turn just for a moment to my second point. We are dealing with the pension plan. I do not suppose there is any member of parliament who would dare, for his own political health, to oppose a form of pension plan at the moment. Why is this so? Well, we have had across this nation the stories for three or four different pension plans. We have seen newspaper headlines so high about the great compromiser. He went to Quebec and met Lesage on the plains of Abraham. They embraced, but we do not know what they whispered to one another. He came back with the great compromise. He is the great diplomat. The fact is that they brought in three plans. Madam Minister, who is not in her place this afternoon, said, I stake my reputation on this plan. Now, she is looking for greener pastures, the leadership of the Liberal party in the province of Ontario. There is one thing I would say in passing, if I may digress for a moment. If she does get that job it ensures the Conservatives another 50 years in office.

He stated, and we refuse to admit that, that the province of Quebec may have been one of the provinces which formed the basis for the establishment of confederation and that, as such, it should be treated as the others, that at the time of the union of the four provinces, it was but one of the four.
The province of Quebec has never accepted and will never accept being treated as one of the ten parts of Canada or of the dominion, as part of confederation. We have contributed to the establishment of confederation. Everybody knows that at the time of the union of Upper Canada and Lower Canada, French Canadians were in majority. However, the situation has changed since then and that is why we do not want to lose our rights and be assimilated by the majority as suggested by the hon. member for Bow River.
He accused the Liberal party of working for centralization but he failed to prove that the Conservative party acted otherwise when it was in power. It had the same attitude during the five years it was in office and even before the Liberals were voted out of office in 1956 or 1957.
It is unfortunate that such speeches are made in the house. It is obvious that the Conservative party has not yet understood the mentality of the province of Quebec and that it does not care for French Canadians. The


latter have learned to know the Conservatives in the past, especially their present leader.
It is not speeches such as the one that the hon. member for Bow River has just made which will strengthen Canadian unity. It is certainly not such speeches that will lead to a better understanding between the two races which served as a basis for our Canadian confederation.
We have been patient too long. We have already made too many concessions to allow ourselves, in 1964, exactly three years before the celebration of confederation, to be insulted or told that we are only one of the ten provinces of Canada-

Mr. Speaker, what we do want, the hon. member for Villeneuve stated it yesterday: we do not want to take anything away from anyone.

We are told to our face in this house that we are but one out of ten provinces within confederation, that we are now but 250,000 people, when actually the province of Quebec has a population of around 6 million. Mr. Speaker, it would be difficult, I think, to have a better example of how far apart two speakers can be in their viewpoints as to the make-up of this nation, some of the constitutional difficulties we face and generally the points of view represented by individuals coming from different parts of the country. Certainly I must confess that the last speaker distressed me a little by some of his comments. I wish he had been a little more specific when he talked about such things as taking away some of the French Canadian's rights, and the too many concessions that French Canada had to make to the rest of the country. If he had put forward a couple of concrete examples of where he thinks the province of Quebec has not been treated right I think he would have had a better chance of achieving some understanding in this house. In my opinion it is perhaps not so important that we know each particular complaint, but when we are now talking about a constitutional amendment to make possible the fulfilment of a pension plan we must realize just how far apart we are in Canada today, how
British North America Act deep seated are some of the feelings and why we need to look very closely not only at our constitutional government but also try to foresee some of the effects which this pension plan is likely to have, where it may impose the stresses and strains that go with change and what it will do to our make-up as one country.
I should like to say to my friend from Quebec that he rather surprises me when he is so indignant about the province of Quebec being called a province rather than a state, and goes on to say that Quebec was formerly regarded as a nation. I must say I had never heard this said before and I am unable to comprehend how he can seriously say that French Canada was ever regarded as a nation. Certainly it was a French colony, just as other parts of Canada were English colonies. These colonies joined together to make one nation. I wish he had explained his reference to Quebec having been formerly regarded as a nation.
With regard to Quebec's special status, certainly it has a special status with respect to its language and its religion and I am sure that the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) would not want to change that in any manner, shape or form. I do not think anyone who accuses the rest of Canada of trying to take away these special French rights is going to find any evidence to support his claim. With regard to whether or not Quebec is just a province, I say that each province in this country is a province with rights in its own house as guaranteed by the constitution. We as a party want to see each province have and maintain its own rights and responsibilities and we want to see that each province, as a political area, has a voice in federal affairs proportionate to its size and population. To that extent each province is different. But since each province has the same rights and obligations and is protected in the same way under the law, it is incorrect to say that any province has a different status other than in the manner I have indicated.
We are here considering an amendment to the constitution with regard to the pension plan, and anyone who looks at the proposed amendment will see that it contains the following provision:
-no such law shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to any such matter.
Every member of the house is familiar with the history of pension legislation as it has been improved from time to time. We have

British North America Act heard many speeches about the fact that the Conservative government made a strenuous effort to secure complete agreement among the provinces /or a constitutional amendment because we did not feel it was wise to attempt to bring in a pension plan without survivor benefits. In other words, we felt if we were going to do the job it should be done right and that therefore first things should come first and we should achieve the consent of the provinces to an amendment.
The Liberals have chosen their own method of proceeding. They thought that political considerations should come first in bringing in a pension plan. They brought one in and we spent considerable time in the house on that first version. They wasted considerable time of the house with a second version. Both versions were of no help to the people of Canada. They simply gave the Liberals a great opportunity for propaganda so that they could say what valiant efforts they were making to bring in a pension plan and so that they could point a finger at others and say: See, they did not do what we can do. They were perfectly right; what they did we did not do. We did not play politics, and they certainly proved they know how to do it.
Those of us who do not have short memories will recall that it was only because the province of Quebec brought out a formula which they sold to the Liberal government that it was possible to avoid a head-on clash and having a so-called pension plan under which provinces would have the power to opt out. Indeed, it looked like we were going to have a so-called Canada pension plan with the two largest provinces out of it altogether.
I bring this up so that we may realize the importance of having agreement, especially with our largest provinces, and so that we may properly settle the background against which we must look at the resolution now before us. In my view, far too little attention has been paid to the fact that with the proposed pension plan, once it starts to work and we get built up in the various provinces large investment funds, there is going to be a great deal of difficulty unless there is some uniformity of investment, some uniformity of agreement among the provinces as to the manner in which these funds can be handled. There is going to be a great deal of difficulty between the federal government and the provinces as to who is going to control them and how much control each is going to have. But I ask the house to consider for one moment the fact that we have different types of gov-


ernment in many of our provinces, that the governments are Liberal, Conservative and Social Credit in the two western provinces, and that the types of leaders of each of these governments in the provinces vary very widely, from some very conservative people, with a small "c" to some who are, I would think, radical.
We know for instance in the province of British Columbia which, in name at least, has a Social Credit government, that the premier of the province has done such things as nationalize a power company, and some of his views on the duties and scope of government intereference with private enterprise come as a little surprising. Frankly, I am never amazed at how widely his views may range in what I call a political sense, all the way from the far left to the far right, and I suggest that with this range of possibility of government action on investment funds there is going to be a tremendous impact on potential investors in Canada-and I am speaking generally. Certainly, no businessman is going to invest his money in an industry in some of the provinces where he has to look seriously at a huge investment fund built up by that province, where the province has not only control over the fund but the ability to direct that fund into a competing business, as well as the ability to make laws and regulations which might cripple him in competition with a government enterprise. This is going to slow down the possibility of investment in Canada. It is going to make this nation almost as risky as some of the, shall I say, unstable Latin American republics. These, I suggest, are not fanciful thoughts at all. The possibility of large government investment funds, coupled with the type of government administration which can become indiscreet from time to time is going to have an effect not just on those industries upon which the government puts its fingers but on every type of investment that might be made in that province, and is something at which all of us should take a long and serious look.
Anyone who has read what the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act provides for regulation of investment of trust funds built up for insurance policies would be aware of the extreme care we take to make sure that those funds cannot be dissipated. We also very carefully regulate, by regulations which were just recently amended, the types of investment. We take a very close look, when they want to amend that act, at the impact on the demand for capital of each of the

various deals in which insurance companies are likely to invest their money. Therefore I say when we are going to contemplate here even vaster sums of money, where there is apparently not at the moment any regulation made by us, where there is very little hope, it seems, that the federal government will be having any control over these investments in a regular pattern, where we have such a wild range and diversity of provinces and have some conception of their different ideas and how wide ranging their regulations for applying those funds may be, we can see the divisive forces which can come about once these funds get going, forces which are really going to wreck this nation. Since we have been able to do so little about our present difficulties in this regard and since we see those difficulties so bitterly expressed as they are today, it is time we gave a little more planning and proceeded more cautiously in putting into force this pension plan no matter how much we may want to see it implemented.

INQUIRIES AS TO FILM RESPECTING PRIME MINISTER-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
I wonder whether hon. members would bear with me if I interrupt the proceedings. I have a duty to perform and I hope it will end in a pleasant way.
Again, it is my duty and obligation to give a definite ruling on certain incidents which took place in the house this morning. This decision could well have been made at the time were it not that such heat had been engendered that it did seem preferable to allow a cooling-off period to elapse so as to permit hon. members to look at things rationally.
As the events to which I refer are still fresh in the minds of each and every one of us, I will not go over them again. However, following an answer from the Prime Minister tne hon. member for Qu'Appelle stated:
On the basis of the evidence we have, I say that it is not the complete truth.
The Prime Minister objected to the words of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and asked the Chair to decide that the hon. member should withdraw the words to the effect that he, the Prime Minister, had not stated the complete truth. At this point, and later on during the debate which followed, in other words twice during the debate, and relying on Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 145 which states-
-it has been formally ruled by Speakers in Canadian Commons that a statement by an honourable member respecting himself and peculiarly within his own knowledge must be accepted-
-I did then, rightly or wrongly, make a decision that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle should withdraw the words he had used and accept the word of the Prime Minister. The actual words I used are as follows:
Therefore, in the circumstances, and in view of the discussion, I would respectfully ask the hon. member for Qu'Appelle to withdraw.
That, evidently, was a decision of the Chair which leads to two conclusions, and they are

Speaker's Ruling
as follows. The first conclusion is to be found in Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 69 and it is:
The Speaker exceeds his authority, if, without having been specially instructed by the house, he takes upon himself to alter any of his rulings which, once given, are under the exclusive control of the house.
The second conclusion follows from the same citation and it is that a Speaker's ruling, once given, belongs to the house which, under standing order 12, is free to reject it.
Also in the same citation it is mentioned that when a member has risen and announced that he appeals from a ruling, no argument should be brought forward to influence the vote about to be given by the house. For the information of the house I wish to refer to Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 133, which reads in part as follows:
When the Speaker takes notice of any expression as personal and disorderly, and tending to introduce heat and confusion, and calls upon the offending member to explain, it is the duty of the latter immediately to explain or retract the offensive expressions.. .The Speaker's demand usually produces the required explanation, at once; if not, the Speaker then repeats the call for explanation, and informs the member, that if he does not immediately respond to it, it will become the duty of the Chair to name him to the house...
Then the first lines of citation 134, paragraph 1, are as follows:
In case a member persists in using unparliamentary language, the Speaker will be compelled to name him, which is equivalent to submitting his conduct to the judgment of the house.
Finally there is a last quotation which I would like to refer to, and it is the first lines of paragraph 2 of citation 55 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which read:
The rulings of the Speaker or chairman must always be respected even though the member against whom they are given may find them arbitrary. If he declines to bow-down and does not appeal to the house he inevitably places himself in the position of having infringed upon the rules of parliamentary practice.
Having stated what the parliamentary practice is and has been throughout the years, I would again ask the hon. member to accept the Prime Minister's word and to withdraw; otherwise the matter will be out of my hands and I will ask the house itself to come to a decision.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO FILM RESPECTING PRIME MINISTER-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning, without any heat in my heart or mind I put myself in your hands. Based on the facts before me at that time, I felt I was correct in making the statement that I did make, and I am afraid I still feel

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO FILM RESPECTING PRIME MINISTER-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
This is a most unpleasant duty, but it is part of my job-
Bight Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
Mr. Speaker, may I say a word on this matter. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken has said that he feels exactly as he did this morning when he made the statement to which you have referred, in which he stated, for the third time, that I had attempted to mislead the house in answer to a question. I took exception to these words, because it was the use of the words "attempted to mislead" which made it a specific and deliberate attempt on my part to mislead the house. I said that was not the case and I appealed to you for a ruling, and Your Honour has given a ruling that the hon. gentleman does not accept.
I hope we can avoid taking any action in this matter by agreement, because it certainly reflects on a ruling of the Chair when a matter of this kind requires that type of action. I know perfectly well that when the hon. gentleman asked his first question it was not addressed to me; it was addressed to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mc-Ilraith), and in looking at the Hansard report I realize now that I should not have intervened at that time and should have waited until a question was addressed to me. To that extent I admit that I was quite wrong and I apologize to the house for that.
But the hon. gentleman made the statement that I had for the third time attempted to mislead the house-and there can be no attempt that is not deliberate. If he had just said I had misled the house it might have been, as was pointed out this morning, an unwitting and unconscious misleading of the house; but an attempt to mislead the house is deliberate. Therefore I had no alternative, as a member of the house, and only in that capacity as a member of the house who should be treated as any other member of the house, no better or no worse, but to take exception to the statement that I had three times attempted to mislead the house in answer to a question. Only in that capacity as a member of the house did I take exception to the statement. But I do express to my hon. friend my regret for having intervened at that time in his question to the President of the Privy Council, which I should not have done.
