subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Port Arthur) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-40, to amend the Broadcasting Act (community antenna).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would have had hopes of withdrawing this bill from the order paper if the government had shown a little more alacrity in facing up to the problem created by community antenna television systems. Some hon. members may recall that on the first of January the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) issued a statement that serious consideration was being given to doing something about this matter. We have had a number of partial statements since and the difficulty still exists. In the time I have I want to put on the record what I think are the two major problems involved in community antenna television systems, and since I have changed my own attitude with regard to one of them I want to be quite clear as to what these two potentials are that are involved in the bill and which I think are essential, whatever action the government takes.
The first question, and the one where I still believe we must have this kind of legislation, relates to the threat to free t.v. or to advertising revenue supported television going into homes that is in prospect as the result of the development of wired systems, and the potential that exists in using them as a network. I think this is a very real threat and it has to be met by the broadcasting authorities, in this case the government agencies.
The second problem, and the one on which I have changed my attitude, really relates to the inroads that C.A.T.V. is making upon the commercial prospects of Canadian stations, particularly in minor markets where C.A.T.V.

Broadcasting Act
brings in a number of American channels and so tends to build a trend whereby the listening audience, the number of homes with television sets that are tuned or can be tuned to the local station and so to the local market, is reduced, and so offers a potential threat to advertising revenue and therefore to the commercial viability of these local stations. The reason I have changed my views in this regard relates partly to a straight recognition of the fact that more than 60 per cent of the television homes in Canada now have, through wired systems and through just sheer closeness to American stations, the ability to have both Canadian and American channels come into their homes. It does not seem to me that at this late date, with 60 per cent of the homes open to this kind of television fare, that we can have the kind of regulation and control based upon some control of the Canadian content, that is, in terms of television stations coming into the community, that might have been envisaged a couple of years ago.
In order to put this matter into what I think is a North American perspective I should like to read from an article that appeared in the New York Times on the 5th of April, 1964. It is headed, "Neighbourly Lines" and it is by a well known authority on television in the United States, Jack Gould. It reads in part as follows:
Nearly one million American families pay a monthly charge to see television and the number could rise with the mushrooming growth of a branch of t.v. probably unknown to the vast majority of viewers.
The relatively novel form of video is known as community antenna television. Originally it was designed as a service for families living in areas where it was difficult or impossible to pick up a station.
But with the technical restlessness characteristic of the electronic business, new applications are being found for community t.v., and there are some who suggest it may prove to be the back door by which pay as you see television might come into being.
Moreover, community t.v. also has been in the headlines because of its potential importance in Austin, Tex., where the system promises to break the local television program monopoly enjoyed for over a decade by station KTBC-TV. KTBC-TV is one of the broadcasting interests of Mrs. Lyndon B. Johnson...
The simplest explanation of community antenna television can be found in the case of a town which is situated deep in a valley with high mountains blocking reception of pictures from distant t.v. stations.
A huge master antenna is erected atop the mountain. Then the pictures from several t.v. stations and the sound from radio stations are sent down the mountainside on wires to a terminal point. From such a terminal more wires fan out

to homes throughout the valley, carrying qualitative pictures and sound into a subscriber's parlour.
The charge for being connected to the community system can vary from 75 cents to $5 a month.
I have known cases in Canada where the charge is as high as $10 a month.
The income goes only to the system operator, not to stations providing its raw material.
At present there are about 1,300 such community systems in 46 states and their construction has become more sophisticated. By use of one or more relay towers between an isolated locale and a t.v. station, it is technically feasible to span almost any distance.
The broadcast industry's eyes really went up when J. Leonard Reinsch, president of the Cox Broadcasting Corporation, announced that he would like to pipe the programs of stations WPIX and WOR in New York halfway across Pennsylvania to the community antenna systems for Tyrone and Chambersburg. The Cox firm also is contemplating the relay of Chicago stations to community systems in Ohio.
I introduce this particular section, which may seem irrelevant, to make a comparison with an application by one community antenna television group to pipe programs all the way from Duluth up to the Winnipeg area, a very great distance, by use of satellite relays.
If, by chance, community systems between New York and Chicago should be linked up, something a prominent Pennsylvania broadcaster.. .fears, there could be the first primitive system of network pay t.v.
The basis for such intriguing speculation is the technical feasibility of using the community t.v. systems as a straight pay as you see t.v. method. In a few instances community antenna operators have done a little of their own programming and some systems have carried sports events blacked out on advertising-sponsored t.v.
I have mentioned this because, at the lake-head, the community antenna television system carried a fight broadcast which was blacked out on free television. I have spoken to Mr. Bassett of the Toronto Maple Leafs about the attitude of that particular firm or company and the national hockey league with regard to this question of major sports events and the likelihood of their disappearing from free t.v. He assured me that as far as he knew there was nothing in it and he would fight against it. But I wish to place on record at this point a part of Dennis Braithwaite's column on December 16, 1963. It covers an interview with Stafford Smythe of the Toronto Maple Leafs hockey club and it goes this way:
The possibility that Saturday night hockey may pass from home screens to become an exclusive pay t.v. attraction is another indication of the shaky economic position of the television industry in this country.

That is all I wish to read from this article. I wanted to slip it into this context. To continue:
But the more Immediate influence of community -t.v. is being felt in areas where there may be only one station on the air, such as Austin. If a community system can double or triple the volume of available t.v., it may not sit well with the one station concerned.
This is the matter about which I have said I have changed my opinion. I no longer see any way in which this can fairly be controlled. It is not for this reason, now, that I would offer this amendment to the Broadcasting Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Is he still advancing this amendment to the Broadcasting Act?

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
Very much so, because I think this threat to free t.v. is very important. I appreciate that the hon. member who intervened comes from Hamilton and I think it was as a result of the Hamilton community antenna television operator coming up here to see him that I had an opportunity of seeing him. He was one of the community-antenna people who was quite prepared to accept these changes of government regulations. He himself could see that this is really the master plan or the great potential of some of the big interests who are interested in promoting and becoming shareholders in community antenna television. If I may read on-
The federal communications commission, which has had a rather ambivalent policy-
Much like the present Minister of Transport's policy.
-on whether it should worry about the economic consequences of its acts, has tried to help the affected station where it could.
I understand the same situation exists in this country as far as the Department of Transport stepping in is concerned.
Thus far it has ruled that such a system should not carry a given t.v. program until the local station, in effect, has exercised a first refusal. But if a community system uses only wires and does not need a relay facility, the agency, at the moment is powerless to act.
This also is the situation in Canada as I understand it.
The larger problem for the F.C.C., of course, is that the agency is confronted with something like two modes of t.v. All its traditional thinking has been directed to the distribution of t.v. broadcast stations requiring channels on the air. Now along comes a supplementary system which could sprawl considerably without recourse to hard-to-get facilities.
Present signs in Washington point to a full-fledged inquiry probably leading to future regula-
Broadcasting Act
tion of all kinds of community antenna t.v_While
the major broadcasting stations are not likely to lose their dominant role the little-noticed community t.v. antenna operator is really sitting pretty. It pay-t.v. and free t.v. come into conflict, he can handle both systems side by side and offer his customers the best of the two video worlds. Which may explain why some of the bigger boys are becoming interested in a system which has introduced another abbreviation into the video vocabulary: "CATV".
The final point I wish to make about United States set-up is this: starting in July, out in California, such a wired network is going into operation, and it will cover all the large networks as well as the broadcasting stations. I suggest to hon. members the question really is whether we are prepared to have the right to regulate-not regulate, now, but to have the right to regulate-in order to make sure that wired television systems do not develop into the kind of provincial or national network which will take off the air free t.v, as we know it. I am prepared to take a position on this. I do not see that there is any great principle involved, but I am prepared to take a position myself. I can see the potential when someone gets to 400,000 or 500,000 wired homes in this country which can be linked up with all Canadian football and national hockey. Some of the greatest entertainment going will disappear from free television airways in favour of these wired arrangements because there is a tremendous money potential there, as anyone who has attended any of the hockey games shown at the theatre in Toronto last winter knows. That field, it seems to me, is a legitimate one. What I am afraid of is the linking of this kind of enterpreneurship and this kind of money with a co-operative or ownership arrangement with the multitude of wire systems which have been developed in this country. I say this is a threat to free television, or advertising revenue sponsored television as we know it, and we need to face up to it at the present time.
I wish to point out that the government is none too clear where it stands. I have a speech here by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) who answers in this field. This speech is called "The Eighth Lively Art". It was made on April 6, 1964 and the hon. minister has something to say about re-broadcasting and pay t.v.
As for pay-t.v., though not yet established firmly as a commercial television system in the home, it has been making strides into the cinemas, as many Ontario hockey fans know very well.

Broadcasting Act
And, after the Etobicoke and Hartford experiments, pay-t.v. is about to get a full trial in California beginning July 1.
As Mr. Ouimet has suggested, t.v. re-broadcasting stations and pay-t.v. require study before situations develop in Canada which may or may not be in the best interests of Canadian broadcasting and the Canadian public.
That is not a very definite position to take. The troika, the three wise men who considered broadcasting and presented reports not long ago, Dr. Stewart, Mr. Jamieson and Mr. Ouiment, went out of their way to leave this problem to the government. Recently, the government announced the setting up of an advisory committee on broadcasting. Again, the terms of reference to this committee specifically say that community antenna television systems are excluded. In other words, the government intends to deal with this. In other words there is an onus upon the government to reach some decision on this matter.
I wish to repeat that two problems are involved. One is the whole future of free television. The other is the effect of the proliferation of community antenna systems upon the economic viability of certain private stations or C.B.C. affiliated stations in small market areas, where the taking away of a sizeable part of the audience could have a disastrous effect, certainly a potentially disastrous effect, on television revenue. I really feel that this bill should be accepted by the government-not as legislation, but I think it should be referred to a committee of this house so that we could hear arguments pro and con.
I wish to make .one final point. I received a letter from a constituent protesting the government's intention to regulate in this field. It is from Mr. Robert Prettie who is president of Northern Wood Preservers Limited, Port Arthur. He said, in effect, the following:
It is surprising, to say the least, that Ottawa is concerned about the effect of cable t.v. on the "commercial health" of our broadcasting system. No concern was shown over the effect of these same stations on cultural attractions, movie theatres or on hockey games. Up until now the public has had a certain freedom of choice within the financial means of the individual to enjoy that freedom.
While I am, naturally, interested in and concerned about the local situation, I am also concerned about the over-all approach and the principles involved. For example, if people in Vancouver, Montreal and Port Arthur can have the services of cable television-why can't the people in Winnipeg have such services? If people in Toronto, Hamilton and Vancouver can receive American television stations direct on their own sets, why should the people of Winnipeg be deprived of

receiving the same programs over cable television if they can get it and if they are prepared to pay for it?
Freedom of the air would seem to me to be just as essential as freedom of the press. However, the present thinking would appear to leave to Ottawa the ultimate decisions as to what will be available to the general public. With so many individual tastes and desires,-do you think that the general public can ever be happy with any selection but their own?
I replied to Mr. Prettie in this form. I want to put it on the record because I think it is relevant to this question:
At least one of the points that you raise was one that I did not take into account, this was lack of any previous concern about the effect of television broadcasting on other cultural attractions and events. The problem in its essence is this (for me and I believe for the government) if cable t.v, systems develop much further, they provide the basis for a potential wired network across the country which could drastically alter what we get on so-called "free television". The battle is already joined in the United States on this. Any action by the government has the intention to stop the development of a network, rather than the creation of any individual community cable system, and I believe this is going to be clarified.
I wrote this letter a few weeks ago, on May 25, when I thought some clarification was coming. Then I went on:
The difference between freedom of the air and freedom of the press is a substantial one. In theory, anyone can start a newspaper or magazine. This is impossible in broadcasting because channels are limited. As you say it would be unfair to deny to others in Canada what many Canadians in other areas receive from American television stations. For that reason, I can no longer, in fairness, oppose the licensing of a cable television system in Winnipeg, but I do oppose the possibility of a network in which Winnipeg is a link with other C.A.T.V. systems and I do advocate a clear order forbidding this as soon as possible.
That in essence sums what is a rather complicated argument on one of the most confusing minor issues that has come into the political arena in the last few months. I have a file of letters here that have come to me, and I am sure most other members can match it. Dozens of people have written about their concern, which has been stirred up through the national community antenna association of Canada. I believe the matter should be solved fairly quickly by a government order to the effect that I have argued this afternoon.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I congratulate the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), the sponsor of this bill, it is for the interest he has shown in this very important matter and the opportunity he is giving us to discuss, in this house, the necessity or inadvisability to submit the community antenna systems and the like to the supervision and control of the board of broad-
Broadcasting Act
cast governors, with the results we know and might expect, especially as regards programming and other non-technical questions.
It is the second time that a motion for second reading of this bill is brought before the house. Last November 29, the hon. member introduced Bill No. C-30, of which Bill No. C-40 now before us is an exact replica. I had the opportunity then to take part in the debate and I am glad today to add new comments to the few remarks I could make before the time allocated to the examination of that proposal had expired.
As the hon. member himself pointed out at the time, it is not sure either that the bill is complete or constitutional and that parliament has the authority to legislate in that respect.
This is a burning question at the present time and it could have great repercussions on Canadian t.v. viewers; it concerns, as well it might, several hon. members. It was discussed in the press throughout the country.
Indeed, all the newspaper accounts I have read were against any measure which would restrict individual freedom. One has to be jealous of one's freedom and be especially alert in that respect these days because governments have taken the habit of enacting legislation and regulations which often infringe upon the fundamental rights of citizens.
Like many others, I received from my constituents several communications showing concern on their part and the desire to get information or to make representations to me. Though a good number of them were perhaps prompted by people who had an interest in the matter, I am sure that many of them wrote to us of their own accord.
However, I can understand, as the hon. member has put it, why he is concerned and disturbed by the fact that these systems may, providing certain circumstances and in certain places, facilitate the reception of American broadcasts and promote the participation of foreign capital in the setting up and managing of corporations or companies which operate systems of that kind.
Since the first bill was introduced and while waiting for the report requested from the board of broadcast governors, the ministers concerned, that is the Minister of Transport and the Secretary of State, then in office, decided to stop issuing licences in some cases, everything following the press release of last December 30. I think that order has now been cancelled. However, since then the requested report was tabled in the house last

Broadcasting Act
March 19 and printed in Hansard. I agree with the hon. member that, in the not too distant future and in the interest of all those concerned in those operations, the government will announce the future policy it intends to follow in that field. Many people or corporations already have invested rather considerable sums of money and are waiting impatiently for the government's decision to proceed. Personally, I feel that this policy or decision will not necessarily follow the recommendations made last March 19 by the joint committee of the board of broadcast governors and the Department of Transport.
I think that many hon. members would be opposed to that body being granted the right to decide what our fellow citizens can see on their television screen, especially when such regulations could apply to only a certain part of the population.
I know that the government, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) are studying that matter seriously, and I am confident that they will find a logical and realistic solution, in keeping with the best interests of Canadians, taking into account the special circumstances surrounding that case, which is very complicated and hard to solve.
The systems involved-and I am still referring only to the community television networks, which in fact are only an extension of the antenna any individual can instal on his house and which are used only to get a better reception of the signals which are already there, in the air, and which play a totally passive role and are no substitute for any television broadcasting of signals-do not transmit any program and, therefore, from the logical and practical viewpoint, cannot be subjected to the same standards and regulations which are provided or set up by radio and television broadcasting stations.
It is one thing to control what programs can be broadcast, but it is another thing to tell the people what programs they will be allowed to watch on their set.
Also, we know that everything that concerns the field of communications is very important here in this country and plays a leading part in what is called "The search for national purposes or objectives".
We must take into serious consideration and not exaggerate the role played by those systems as regards the transmission of signals coming from our neighbours to the south. As

a matter of fact, 30 per cent of all cable systems in Canada do not transmit signals from the United States, but are used only to provide a variety and an improvement of programs already picked up in an area, or else they increase the capacity to pick up programs of Canadian stations which could not be seen otherwise.
Moreover, the subscribers of these networks represent only 5 per cent of all homes having television and even in this small percentage, one has to take into account all those who, like myself, live near the American border and can pick up television shows with an ordinary antenna or even without any.
It is obvious that in our country, the great majority of our people are concentrated in more or less narrow strips of land in the southern part of the country along the borders and can easily pick up the powerful American television stations. Such is the case in the eastern townships and except channel 7, the excellent station operated by the newspaper La Tribune in Sherbrooke, we can easily pick up American channels but hardly French and English stations of Montreal if we did not have the cable transmission services which are much appreciated by some 20,000 subscribers to the dozen of networks operating in our area.
Such is the situation of about half of the Canadian people. Regulations restricting the freedom and rights of a class of citizens would, in my opinion, only be unfair and discriminatory.
We appreciate the efforts and the contribution of the national network and of all private stations which are indispensable to us, and we acknowledge their merits. They actually offer us several interesting programs which are sometimes of great value.
It must be recognized, however, that our fellow citizens often look at programs originating south of the border and which our neighbours, with their unlimited means and greater facilities in every respect, can offer us in a more complete and elaborate manner.
At a time when, as evidenced by the Tel-star experience, we shall soon be able to see programs coming from any country in the world, television viewers in Canada should not be prevented from seeing programs of interest to them. In my opinion, attempts should be made rather to encourage, help and prompt the C.B.C. network, as well as t.v. and radio stations and our artists, to present choice programs of prime quality and likely to hold the attention of Canadians who,

in general, are interested in their country, in their culture, in our projects, in our artists, and who gladly watch our programs when they satisfy their legitimate aspirations.
That solution would perhaps be more practical, more realistic and easier to apply. I know that we are already immensely contributing towards the operations of the C.B.C., the national film board, etc., corporations promoting a Canadian culture and a Canadian mentality, but we sometimes wonder if the best means are being taken to achieve this highly desirable purpose.
I do not want to imply that I am against all controls; wire television systems now have to comply with regulations established by the Department of Transport which controls the issuance of licences and which can, beforehand, give particular attention to stations receiving and relaying programs, the area covered, etc., and, above all, it is reasonable to expect that those networks have the obligation to broadcast Canadian programs when it is technically possible to do so.
I have no objection either to corporations or companies which operate such systems and want to obtain a licence being owned and controlled by Canadian interests in a large proportion, if not entirely.
However, we must avoid passing regulations that would deprive an individual of the right to watch on his t.v. set what he might pick up himself by using or erecting a more expensive aerial, which he avoids by becoming a subscriber to a community system. A regulation to the contrary would be an undesirable change. Our present legislation provides and assures that our country has broadcasting means under Canadian control and requiring a certain amount of Canadian content.
The objectives and purposes mentioned in section 10 of the Broadcasting Act passed in 1958 certainly did not forbid to listen to or watch programs from foreign countries, in order to seal off our culture against outside influence, when on the contrary it can develop and improve through contact with the views and the clash of ideas from all parts of the world.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-40 before the house this afternoon, the purpose of which is to give the board of broadcast governors some control over the so-called community antenna t.v. and cable systems which are regularly picking up broadcast programs and relaying
Broadcasting Act
them for profit by cable to private homes, is one which I think needs to be studied by a committee of this house to determine whether or not this bill provides the manner in which it should be controlled or whether some other appropriate means should be set up. I say that for the reason that up to the present time the Department of Transport has exercised some control over the establishment of cable television systems, but at the same time I do not believe there has been an adequate or clear concept of how they do in fact go about setting up such control. As I understand it, they simply issue a licence or refuse to issue a licence to instal a cable system in a city, and that is about as far as it goes.
A few months ago a hearing lasting several days was held in the city of Ottawa at which the television and cable relay people all over the country presented their views. I think it is fair to say that at that time the main contention they put forward at the hearing was that these groups were nothing more or less than a large antenna system. In other words, a large number of people had banded together in a co-operative effort which resulted in their being able to receive programs which, in fact, they could individually receive anyway.
When the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) introduced this bill, he mentioned that there was some confusion surrounding the regulations and the actual functions of this cable television system. I believe he said a mouthful when he said that. There are so many conflicting interests and conflicting regulations when you consider how this is going to affect private television, but certainly the House of Commons ought to give some consideration to it. I believe an agency of government should be concerned, in fact has an obligation to be concerned, when there are large segments of the Canadian population who may be deprived of something such as free television. In addition to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Port Arthur, I think we should very carefully consider the implication in rural areas as opposed to urban areas. We should consider what would happen if free television were either downgraded or discontinued. In many areas, even in my own constituency, there are people who are objecting vigorously to the establishment of cable television. They feel that, if and when it is installed, it is certainly going to delay the day when other satellites are set up in the area. This would

Broadcasting Act
mean the people in rural areas would be denied the opportunity of listening to more than one channel.
Most of my constituency, which may or may not be typical, is confined to one channel television. It happens that the C.B.C. serves both ends of the constituency from two different broadcast areas. I know that large numbers of these people feel their interests are being hurt by the establishment of cable television because this is going to pick up all these urban customers, if you want to call them that, and there would be no commercial incentive to establish free broadcasting satellites.
I do not want to take up too much time, but I do believe that the expansion of cable television in Canada has reached the point where we have to recognize the fact that the regulation for the 55 per cent Canadian content in programming is being defeated. In other words, if it is possible, and we know now it is, to bring into these cable systems the entire programming of a United States station for one day, then these Canadian listeners do not get any Canadian content in their programs. I believe that this subject should be referred to a committee, and we should re-examine the regulation calling for 55 per cent Canadian content. If we are going to insist that private television stations in the country have 55 per cent Canadian content in their programs, whether or not their audience likes it, then in my opinion it is not fair that cable television should be allowed to broadcast the complete program schedule of stations which are not required to have that 55 per cent Canadian content. On the one hand, perhaps we have too little control, and on the other hand we are insisting on too much control.
I think perhaps we could argue that in certain areas satellites serve almost exactly the same purpose as cable television. In other words a satellite broadcasting 50 miles or 100 miles away from some major city into a small town or rural area is simply relaying the programs that originate in a television station in a city some distance away. The argument that there should be some local programming for that area is not valid at all, because of the point of origin of the program.
I do not wish to say any more, Mr. Speaker, except that I support the suggestion by the hon. member for Fort Arthur that a committee of this house neds to have a look at this cable television development in Canada in view of the tremendous expansion of it. I

agree with him also that there is a danger -I think that was the main basis of his argument-that it might develop into a closed circuit network from one end of the country to the other. Certainly if this happens I can see no difference between the control that should be exercised on that network and the control that should be exercised over private television networks. I am not sure that 1 can accept the bill that is before us, because it does seem to give blanket control to the board of broadcast governors over cable television without any indication as to what the members of the House of Commons would like to have done. I think it would be better if the subject were referred to a committee to be studied, and then recommendations made by the members of this house as to the regulations that should govern.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with considerable interest to the comments of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). I think many of the things he said are quite correct, and they are receiving the attention of the government.
The only area in which the hon. member became critical of the government, at least so far as I could ascertain, was that it could have moved faster in this area; but possibly the hon. member himself suggested a good reason why the government has not moved faster. Although the regulations in the Radio Act are holding the line adequately for the present, he himself indicated that he has been having second thoughts on this very complicated matter, and that is one of the reasons

why the government itself has not moved so fast in this area.
The hon. member indicated what is going through his mind on the basis of second thoughts, on the question of C.A.T.V. providing competition or cutting into broadcasting stations' service, and the implications that flow from this. He has indicated he is not so much concerned about this any more, and to a degree the matter gets down to the more technical aspects of the question with respect to C.A.T.V., and with respect to which is the most competent body or agency to deal with these matters, and with respect to what the technical criteria should be.
Perhaps there is some merit in what the hon. member suggests when he states he would bring that authority under the B.B.G. At the present time the Radio Act does provide some control. The hon. member did not deal with the question of foreign ownership to any great extent, at least that I heard, and I think this is one of the most serious matters concerned.
As I understand it, the Radio Act at present provides for a minimum of 75 per cent home ownership or partly Canadian ownership, and 25 per cent non-residential foreign ownership, and many people, including myself, have serious doubts whether this ownership provision is at all adequate. A lot can be said, especially when there is expensive technical equipment to purchase, in favour of a United States company purchasing 25 per cent of the equity stock in any C.A.T.V. network and, with the adequate financing they have, that they in fact should have the managerial control of the company. There is some question as to whether the provision in the Radio Act is sufficient to maintain Canadian ownership of C.A.T.V. This is very important, due to the fear that has been expressed, not only by the mover of this bill but by other hon. members who have spoken, regarding the implications of a possible network throughout the country.
We also have to be very concerned about foreign ownership because of the fact that these people might bid on something that is really Canadian, something like hockey night in Canada, and if this would happen we would have cause for real concern. I believe the government would be well advised to consider this bill, but to do so in conjunction with an over-all communications policy, not only in so far as foreign ownership of
Broadcasting Act
C.A.T.V. is concerned but with reference to television generally and radio as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put on the record a few comments by a man who has written to me on this subject. He is the operator of one of these C.A.T.V. stations in my constituency, Mr. Norman Curry, and in his letter he says he is concerned about the possibility of Famous Players buying into C.A.T.V. operations across the country. I do not think there can be any doubt about who owns Famous Players. It is foreign owned and is having very significant influence in the C.A.T.V. field, and in the national association to which the hon. member referred.
In his letter he states:
With this in mind, I am taking the liberty of putting my views forward, and I came here to give warning that if Famous Players are allowed to purchase and control cable systems across Canada, without any regulation, then the government is faced with the possibility of a third network in Canada, completely controlled by American sources. This is not a far fetched statement. Technically, all the systems that Famous Players now own or operate, or can purchase in the future, are capable of being interconnected. Various means exist in Canada that can be used to accomplish this purpose.
The Bell Telephone Company of Canada, the Canadian National Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway each possess micro-wave facilities, and wire facilities, licensed by the dominion government as common carriers, at the service of those who wish to pay the fee.
So that in the event Famous Players decided to interconnect their systems, through these organizations, the use of their facilities, the number of viewers that they will have as a captive audience, and if a method of charging for a program placed on these facilities was carried out, they would be able to outbid any Canadian broadcaster in Canada, including the C.B.C., in the purchase of entertainment.
If the government wishes programs for Canadians to be determined by Americans or for that matter, by private Canadian interests across Canada, then there will be no regulations. If this occurs, I firmly believe that within a matter of a very few years, Famous Players Corporation, with the assets available to them, and their resources will succeed in removing the Saturday night hockey games from Maple Leaf Gardens, from the reach of Canadian broadcasters, and place it on their own system for a few.
But if the government believes that Canadian programming should be operated by Canadians for Canadians, then we must have regulations, and one of the keys to the whole situation is the interconnection between cable systems across Canada.
